concept.name: Liquidation bonus
concept.definition: The liquidation bonus (or penalty) is the discount at which a liquidator can claim a borrower's collateral when repaying their debt — the economic incentive that makes third-party liquidation profitable.
concept.intuition: It is the bounty for the repo agent: repay part of a failing loan and you get to buy the borrower's collateral at a few percent below market.
concept.mechanics: When HF < 1, anyone can call liquidationCall, repay up to 50% of the debt (100% if HF is below the close-factor threshold), and receive collateral worth debt repaid × (1 + bonus). Bonuses are set per asset by governance (e.g. ~5% on majors, higher on risky assets); the discount is the borrower's liquidation penalty.
concept.formula: Collateral seized = (debt repaid × (1 + liquidation bonus)) / collateral price; e.g. repay $1,000 at 5% bonus → $1,050 of collateral.
concept.failure_modes: Bonuses that are too small fail to attract liquidators in congestion or crashes (bad debt accumulates); too large, and they over-punish borrowers and invite liquidation-hunting manipulation of oracle prices.
concept.misconceptions: The bonus is not free money for liquidators — competition, gas costs and price slippage on seized collateral eat most of it. Borrowers lose the bonus on top of their market losses; it is a penalty, not a fee rebate.
concept.example: A liquidator repays $5,000 of a failing loan backed by ETH at a 5% bonus and receives $5,250 worth of the borrower's ETH, profiting ~$250 minus gas and any slippage when selling the ETH.

citations.source: Frangella & Herskind, Aave V3 Technical Paper (2022)
citations.section: Section 3-4: risk parameters (LTV, liquidation threshold, liquidation bonus)
